module_title: Vicarious Liability, Sovereign Immunity & Joint Tortfeasors
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams, Judiciary, and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores the complex doctrines where one person is held liable for the wrong done by another, and dissects the intricate liability of the State in India.

core_concepts.title: Vicarious Liability (Master and Servant)
core_concepts.description:
Normally, a person is only liable for their own wrongs. Vicarious Liability makes a Master liable for the torts committed by their Servant in the **'course of employment'**.
Based on two maxims:
1. *Qui facit per alium facit per se*: He who acts through another is deemed in law to do it himself.
2. *Respondeat Superior*: Let the principal/superior be liable.

core_concepts.title: Course of Employment
core_concepts.description:
A master is liable even if the servant acted carelessly, mistakenly, or wilfully, provided the act falls within the 'course of employment'.
- Fraud by Servant: In *Lloyd v. Grace, Smith & Co.*, a managing clerk defrauded a client. The firm was held vicariously liable because the clerk was acting within the scope of his apparent authority, even though he acted for his own criminal benefit.

core_concepts.title: Independent Contractor vs. Servant
core_concepts.description:
A master is liable for a servant, but generally NOT liable for an independent contractor.
- Test of Control: A servant is told *what* to do and *how* to do it (Master has control). An independent contractor is told *what* to do, but decides *how* to do it (No control over the method).
- Exceptions: A person IS liable for an independent contractor if the work itself involves a strict liability or non-delegable duty (e.g., hazardous activities).

core_concepts.title: State Liability and Sovereign Immunity (Article 300)
core_concepts.description:
Can the Government of India be sued for the torts of its employees?
- Sovereign Functions: Functions that can only be performed by the State (e.g., defense, administration of justice, maintenance of law and order, police arresting someone). The State is **NOT liable** for torts committed by employees performing sovereign functions (*Kasturilal Ralia Ram v. State of UP* - police stole confiscated gold).
- Non-Sovereign Functions: Commercial or welfare functions (e.g., running a hospital, repairing roads). The State **IS liable** here (*State of Rajasthan v. Vidyawati* - a government jeep ran over a pedestrian).

important_entities.name: Joint Tortfeasors
important_entities.key_fact: Multiple people acting in concert to commit a tort.
important_entities.significance: When two or more persons commit a tort acting together in furtherance of a common design, they are 'Joint Tortfeasors'. Their liability is **joint and several**, meaning the plaintiff can sue any one of them for the full amount, or all of them together.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Advanced exams test the modern validity of the *Kasturilal* judgment. Over time, the Supreme Court has heavily restricted the 'Sovereign Immunity' defense to protect fundamental rights. In *Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa* (custodial death), the court awarded compensation against the State under public law, sidestepping the sovereign immunity defense of traditional tort law.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Qui Facit = Who Acts; Respondeat = Superior Answers
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Associate *Qui Facit* with the justification of the act (acting through an agent), and *Respondeat Superior* with the destination of liability (the boss pays).

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Law Optional or Judiciary Mains, when discussing State Liability under Article 300, always contrast the **Vidyawati case** (liability upheld for non-sovereign act) with the **Kasturilal case** (liability denied for sovereign act), and conclude with modern constitutional remedies (Nilabati Behera).
